claim: MCR-1 mediated colistin resistance in Escherichia coli is due to modified LPS at the cytoplasmic rather than outer membrane.
source: We discovered that MCR-1 mediated colistin resistance in Escherichia coli is due to modified LPS at the cytoplasmic rather than OM.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding as a discovery from the study.

claim: Colistin exerts bactericidal activity by targeting LPS in the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: We discovered that MCR-1 mediated colistin resistance in Escherichia coli is due to modified LPS at the cytoplasmic rather than OM. In doing so, we also demonstrated that colistin exerts bactericidal activity by targeting LPS in the cytoplasmic membrane (CM).
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as a demonstrated finding from the study.

claim: Murepavadin causes LPS accumulation in the cytoplasmic membrane of Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
source: Using the LPS transport inhibitor murepavadin, we were able to cause LPS accumulation in the CM of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which resulted in increased susceptibility to colistin in vitro and improved treatment efficacy in vivo.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from the study.

claim: LPS accumulation in the cytoplasmic membrane results in increased susceptibility to colistin in vitro.
source: Using the LPS transport inhibitor murepavadin, we were able to cause LPS accumulation in the CM of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which resulted in increased susceptibility to colistin in vitro and improved treatment efficacy in vivo.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from the study.

claim: Combination of murepavadin and colistin improves treatment efficacy in vivo.
source: Using the LPS transport inhibitor murepavadin, we were able to cause LPS accumulation in the CM of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which resulted in increased susceptibility to colistin in vitro and improved treatment efficacy in vivo.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from the study.

claim: Colistin and polymyxin B are two closely related polymyxin antibiotics used clinically.
source: Two closely related polymyxin antibiotics are used clinically, colistin (polymyxin E) and polymyxin B, which share a high degree of structural similarity, consisting of a cationic peptide ring of 7 amino acids connected to a hydrophobic acyl tail by a linear chain of three amino acids (Velkov et al., 2010; Biswas et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Polymyxins consist of a cationic peptide ring of 7 amino acids connected to a hydrophobic acyl tail by a linear chain of three amino acids.
source: Two closely related polymyxin antibiotics are used clinically, colistin (polymyxin E) and polymyxin B, which share a high degree of structural similarity, consisting of a cationic peptide ring of 7 amino acids connected to a hydrophobic acyl tail by a linear chain of three amino acids (Velkov et al., 2010; Biswas et al., 2012).
evidence: This structural description is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Up to 70% of patients fail to respond to colistin treatment.
source: Polymyxins are rapidly bactericidal towards Gram-negative bacteria in vitro but are considerably less efficacious in vivo, with up to 70% of patients failing to respond to colistin treatment (Falagas et al., 2010; Paul et al., 2018; Linden et al., 2003).
evidence: This clinical observation is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Only 50% of people with normal renal function achieve a steady state serum concentration of polymyxins sufficient to kill bacteria.
source: Restrictions on dosage due to the nephrotoxicity of polymyxins mean that only 50% of people with normal renal function achieve a steady state serum concentration sufficient to kill bacteria (Tran et al., 2016; Satlin et al., 2020).
evidence: This clinical observation is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The binding of polymyxins to lipopolysaccharide on the surface of Gram-negative bacteria leads to disruption of the outer membrane.
source: Whilst it is well established that the binding of polymyxins to lipopolysaccharide (LPS) on the surface of Gram-negative bacteria leads to disruption of the outer membrane (OM), it is unclear how this results in cell lysis and bacterial death (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Biswas et al., 2012; MacNair et al., 2018).
evidence: This mechanism is described as well established and supported by citations.

claim: Polymyxins permeabilise the cytoplasmic membrane, which is required for bacterial lysis and killing.
source: Once across the OM, polymyxins permeabilise the cytoplasmic membrane (CM), which is required for bacterial lysis and killing (Velkov et al., 2010; Garg et al., 2017; Biswas et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The mechanism by which colistin damages the cytoplasmic membrane is unclear.
source: However, the mechanism by which colistin damages the CM is unclear (Powers and Hancock, 2003; Trimble et al., 2016).
evidence: This gap in knowledge is explicitly stated and supported by citations.

claim: Polymyxins can interact with mammalian cell membranes, leading to changes in epithelial monolayer permeability.
source: In support of this, polymyxins can interact with mammalian cell membranes, leading to changes in epithelial monolayer permeability (Berg et al., 1996).
evidence: This observation is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Polymyxin antibiotics have some inhibitory activity against Streptococcus pyogenes.
source: Polymyxin antibiotics also have some inhibitory activity against the Gram-positive bacterium Streptococcus pyogenes, where the CM is formed of a phospholipid bilayer (Betts et al., 2016).
evidence: This observation is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: The concentrations of polymyxin B required to disrupt mammalian epithelial cells or inhibit the growth of S. pyogenes (8–16 µg ml−1) are above typical serum concentrations of the antibiotic.
source: Firstly, the concentrations of polymyxin B required to disrupt mammalian epithelial cells or inhibit the growth of S. pyogenes (8–16 µg ml−1) are above typical serum concentrations of the antibiotic, and colistin at clinically relevant concentrations displays no activity against other Gram-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus or Enterococcus faecalis (Berg et al., 1996; Betts et al., 2016; Si et al., 2018; Kouidhi et al., 2011).
evidence: This observation is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Colistin has very little activity against synthetic phospholipid bilayer membranes unless LPS is present.
source: Furthermore, colistin has very little activity against synthetic phospholipid bilayer membranes unless LPS is present, a finding that explains why polymyxins are 30–100-fold less active against colistin-resistant Acinetobacter baumanii isolates that are LPS-deficient, with an OM composed of a phospholipid bilayer (Khadka et al., 2018; Moffatt et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This observation is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Polymyxins are 30–100-fold less active against colistin-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii isolates that are LPS-deficient.
source: Furthermore, colistin has very little activity against synthetic phospholipid bilayer membranes unless LPS is present, a finding that explains why polymyxins are 30–100-fold less active against colistin-resistant Acinetobacter baumanii isolates that are LPS-deficient, with an OM composed of a phospholipid bilayer (Khadka et al., 2018; Moffatt et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This observation is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations show that the interaction of colistin with phospholipid bilayers is unlike what has been reported for other antimicrobial peptides that target phospholipid bilayers.
source: Finally, molecular dynamics simulations show that the interaction of colistin with phospholipid bilayers is unlike what has been reported for other antimicrobial peptides that target phospholipid bilayers (Fu et al., 2020).
evidence: This finding is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: LPS is synthesised in the cytoplasm via the Raetz pathway and introduced into the inner leaflet of the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: In Gram-negative bacteria, LPS is synthesised in the cytoplasm via the Raetz pathway, during which it is introduced into the inner leaflet of the CM (Raetz et al., 2007; Simpson and Trent, 2019).
evidence: This biochemical pathway is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: LPS is flipped to the outer leaflet of the cytoplasmic membrane by MsbA.
source: It is then flipped to the outer leaflet of the CM by MsbA before transportation to the OM via the LptABCDEFG machinery (Okuda et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 1998; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This transport mechanism is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LPS is transported to the outer membrane via the LptABCDEFG machinery.
source: It is then flipped to the outer leaflet of the CM by MsbA before transportation to the OM via the LptABCDEFG machinery (Okuda et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 1998; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This transport mechanism is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Ten mobile colistin resistance (mcr) gene variants have been described.
source: To date, 10 mobile colistin resistance (mcr) gene variants have been described, all of which encode phosphoethanolamine (pEtN) transferases that modify the lipid A component of LPS with pEtN as it is trafficked through the CM on the way to the OM (Liu et al., 2016; Carroll et al., 2019; Nang et al., 2019; Skov and Monnet, 2016; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MCR proteins encode phosphoethanolamine transferases that modify the lipid A component of LPS with pEtN as it is trafficked through the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: To date, 10 mobile colistin resistance (mcr) gene variants have been described, all of which encode phosphoethanolamine (pEtN) transferases that modify the lipid A component of LPS with pEtN as it is trafficked through the CM on the way to the OM (Liu et al., 2016; Carroll et al., 2019; Nang et al., 2019; Skov and Monnet, 2016; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Colistin resistance can arise via mutations in genes encoding two-component regulatory systems such as PhoPQ, PmrAB, or BasRS.
source: Colistin resistance can also arise via mutations in genes encoding two-component regulatory systems such as PhoPQ, PmrAB, or BasRS (Poirel et al., 2017; Janssen et al., 2020).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mutations in two-component regulatory systems typically lead to the addition of 4-amino-4-deoxy-l-arabinose (L-ara4N) and/or pEtN groups to LPS at the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: This typically leads to the addition of 4-amino-4-deoxy-l-arabinose (L-ara4N) and/or pEtN groups to LPS, with this modification also occurring at the CM (Simpson and Trent, 2019; Poirel et al., 2017).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Colistin permits ingress of the N-phenyl-1-napthylamine (NPN) fluorophore into the outer membrane of E. coli expressing mcr-1.
source: For example, colistin has been shown to permit ingress of the N-phenyl-1-napthylamine (NPN) fluorophore into the OM of E. coli expressing mcr-1 (MacNair et al., 2018).
evidence: This observation is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Colistin greatly enhances the activity of hydrophobic antibiotics such as rifampicin against polymyxin-resistant bacteria via disruption of the outer membrane.
source: Furthermore, colistin greatly enhances the activity of hydrophobic antibiotics such as rifampicin against polymyxin-resistant bacteria via disruption of the OM (Brennan-Krohn et al., 2018).
evidence: This observation is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Despite colistin damaging the outer membrane of resistant bacteria, it is unable to kill or lyse them.
source: However, despite colistin damaging the OM of resistant bacteria, it is unable to kill or lyse them (MacNair et al., 2018).
evidence: This observation is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: E. coli MC1000 expressing mcr-1 had a colistin MIC of 2 µg ml−1 compared to 0.25 µg ml−1 for the pEmpty control strain.
source: As expected, we found that E. coli MC1000 expressing mcr-1 had a significantly greater colistin minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC, 2 µg ml−1) compared to the MC1000 pEmpty control strain (0.25 µg ml−1), which was similar to that seen for clinical isolates (Dortet et al., 2018; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 42 ± 19% of total cellular LPS from MCR-1-producing E. coli was unmodified.
source: Of note, whilst 42 ± 19% of total cellular LPS from MCR-1-producing E. coli was unmodified, the proportion of unmodified LPS in the CM was just 21 ± 2% (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This quantitative result is directly stated and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The proportion of unmodified LPS in the cytoplasmic membrane of MCR-1-producing E. coli was 21 ± 2%.
source: Of note, whilst 42 ± 19% of total cellular LPS from MCR-1-producing E. coli was unmodified, the proportion of unmodified LPS in the CM was just 21 ± 2% (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This quantitative result is directly stated and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Colistin caused permeabilisation of the outer membrane of E. coli pEmpty strain in a dose-dependent manner.
source: As expected, colistin caused permeabilisation of the OM of the E. coli pEmpty strain in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1B).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Colistin disrupted the outer membrane of E. coli expressing mcr-1 to a similar degree to E. coli pEmpty.
source: In agreement with previous findings, we found that colistin also disrupted the OM of E. coli expressing mcr-1 to a similar degree to E. coli pEmpty (Figure 1B; MacNair et al., 2018).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated, shown in Figure 1B, and supported by citation.

claim: Colistin sensitised E. coli expressing mcr-1 to rifampicin with a fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) value of 0.14.
source: However, in keeping with previous work, we found that colistin sensitised E. coli expressing mcr-1 to rifampicin, with a fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) value of 0.14 indicating synergy between the two antibiotics in a checkerboard assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 6; MacNair et al., 2018).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6, and supported by citation.

claim: Colistin exposure resulted in a strong PI signal from E. coli pEmpty cells, indicative of cytoplasmic membrane permeabilisation.
source: As expected, colistin exposure resulted in a strong PI signal from E. coli pEmpty cells, indicative of CM permeabilisation (Figure 1C), which gradually declined, most likely due to nucleases released from lysed bacteria (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The cytoplasmic membrane of E. coli expressing mcr-1 remained intact during colistin exposure, as demonstrated by the lack of PI-mediated fluorescence.
source: However, despite colistin permeabilising the OM of E. coli expressing mcr-1, the CM of these bacteria remained intact, as demonstrated by the lack of PI-mediated fluorescence (Figure 1C).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Colistin caused lysis of E. coli pEmpty cells, as seen by a reduction in OD595nm readings over time.
source: In keeping with these findings, colistin caused lysis of E. coli pEmpty cells, as seen by a reduction in OD595nm readings over time (Figure 1D).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: E. coli cells producing MCR-1 grew in the presence of colistin despite the damage the polymyxin caused to the outer membrane.
source: By contrast, E. coli cells producing MCR-1 grew in the presence of colistin despite the damage the polymyxin caused to the OM, as demonstrated by an increase in OD595nm measurements over time (Figure 1D).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There were no differences in fluidity of the cytoplasmic membrane between E. coli pEmpty or mcr-1-expressing cells.
source: There were no differences in fluidity of the CM between E. coli pEmpty or mcr-1-expressing cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a slight increase in the positive charge of the cytoplasmic membrane of mcr-1-expressing E. coli relative to the pEmpty control.
source: As might be expected, there was a slight increase in the positive charge of the CM of the mcr-1-expressing E. coli relative to the pEmpty control, indicative of the presence of cationic pEtN modifications to LPS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cytoplasmic membrane of spheroplasts of E. coli MC1000 mcr-1 was resistant to damage by colistin.
source: In the absence of treatment, there was a small but progressive loss of CM integrity over time due to the fragile nature of spheroplasts. However, allowing for this, the CM of spheroplasts of E. coli MC1000 mcr-1 was resistant to damage by colistin, but susceptible to daptomycin and nisin (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figures 2A-C.

claim: The cytoplasmic membrane of spheroplasts of E. coli MC1000 mcr-1 was susceptible to daptomycin and nisin.
source: In the absence of treatment, there was a small but progressive loss of CM integrity over time due to the fragile nature of spheroplasts. However, allowing for this, the CM of spheroplasts of E. coli MC1000 mcr-1 was resistant to damage by colistin, but susceptible to daptomycin and nisin (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figures 2A-C.

claim: Colistin, daptomycin, and nisin all permeabilised the cytoplasmic membrane of spheroplasts of E. coli pEmpty.
source: By contrast, colistin, daptomycin, and nisin all permeabilised the CM of spheroplasts of E. coli pEmpty (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figures 2A-C.

claim: Colistin, daptomycin, and nisin all caused lysis of spheroplasts of E. coli pEmpty.
source: In keeping with the data from assays measuring CM damage, colistin, daptomycin, and nisin all caused lysis of spheroplasts of E. coli pEmpty, whilst the spheroplasts from E. coli expressing mcr-1 were undamaged by colistin, but were lysed by both daptomycin and nisin (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figures 2D-F.

claim: Spheroplasts from E. coli expressing mcr-1 were undamaged by colistin, but were lysed by both daptomycin and nisin.
source: In keeping with the data from assays measuring CM damage, colistin, daptomycin, and nisin all caused lysis of spheroplasts of E. coli pEmpty, whilst the spheroplasts from E. coli expressing mcr-1 were undamaged by colistin, but were lysed by both daptomycin and nisin (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figures 2D-F.

claim: The protection afforded to the cytoplasmic membrane by MCR-1 is specific for colistin.
source: Combined, these data demonstrated that the protection afforded to the CM by MCR-1 is specific for colistin, and that the polymyxin antibiotic does not share the same target as the phospholipid-targeting CAMPs.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing differential effects of colistin versus daptomycin and nisin.

claim: There is a clear dose-dependent relationship between the abundance of unmodified LPS in the cytoplasmic membrane and the susceptibility of spheroplasts to colistin-mediated cytoplasmic membrane damage and lysis.
source: To further explore the specificity of MCR-1-mediated LPS modifications in the CM for protection against colistin, we produced spheroplasts of E. coli with different levels of LPS modification. This revealed a clear dose-dependent relationship between the abundance of unmodified LPS in the CM and the susceptibility of spheroplasts to colistin-mediated CM damage and lysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Magnesium chloride conferred dose-dependent protection from colistin-mediated cytoplasmic membrane disruption.
source: In keeping with a role for cation bridges, we found that magnesium chloride conferred dose-dependent protection from colistin-mediated CM disruption (Figure 3A).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Identical concentrations of sodium chloride did not protect spheroplasts from colistin.
source: To rule out a general protective osmotic effect from the higher salt concentration, we demonstrated that identical concentrations of sodium chloride did not protect spheroplasts from colistin (Figure 3B).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The presence of exogenous magnesium had no significant effect on reducing spheroplast cytoplasmic membrane damage caused by daptomycin or nisin.
source: Furthermore, the presence of exogenous magnesium had no significant effect on reducing spheroplast CM damage caused by daptomycin or nisin (Figure 3C,D), confirming that these CAMPs do not have the same CM target as colistin.
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: Colistin synergised with murepavadin against P. aeruginosa PA14 cells with a FICI value of 0.375.
source: To test our hypothesis, we first used a checkerboard MIC assay and found that colistin synergised with murepavadin against P. aeruginosa PA14 cells (FICI value of 0.375), revealing that sub-lethal concentrations of the LptD inhibitor sensitised the bacterium to colistin (Figure 4A; Odds, 2003).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Sub-lethal concentrations of murepavadin caused a slight reduction in LPS levels in the outer membrane of P. aeruginosa cells.
source: Sub-lethal concentrations of murepavadin caused a slight reduction in LPS levels in the OM of P. aeruginosa cells, but a significant increase in the amount of LPS in the CM compared to untreated spheroplasts (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Sub-lethal concentrations of murepavadin caused a significant increase in the amount of LPS in the cytoplasmic membrane of P. aeruginosa compared to untreated spheroplasts.
source: Sub-lethal concentrations of murepavadin caused a slight reduction in LPS levels in the OM of P. aeruginosa cells, but a significant increase in the amount of LPS in the CM compared to untreated spheroplasts (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Colistin permeabilised the outer membrane of P. aeruginosa to the same extent in bacteria exposed or not exposed to murepavadin.
source: Despite the slight reduction of LPS at the OM caused by murepavadin, colistin permeabilised the OM to the same extent as bacteria that had not been exposed to murepavadin, with similar levels of NPN uptake (Figure 4B).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Murepavadin significantly enhanced permeabilisation of the cytoplasmic membrane by colistin in whole cells of P. aeruginosa.
source: By contrast, however, murepavadin significantly enhanced permeabilisation of the CM by colistin in whole cells of P. aeruginosa, as determined via uptake of PI (Figure 4C).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: P. aeruginosa cells exposed to murepavadin were more rapidly lysed by colistin than untreated cells.
source: Furthermore, P. aeruginosa cells exposed to murepavadin were more rapidly lysed by colistin than untreated cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There was no synergy observed between murepavadin and PMBN, with an FICI value of 1.
source: To test this, we first examined whether the OM permeabilising agent polymyxin B nonapeptide (PMBN) also synergised with murepavadin. However, we did not see synergy in MIC checkerboard or bactericidal assays between PMBN and murepavadin (Figure 4—figure supplement 5, Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Murepavadin pre-treated spheroplasts were much more susceptible to colistin-induced cytoplasmic membrane damage and lysis than untreated spheroplasts.
source: Next, we pre-treated P. aeruginosa with murepavadin alone to cause LPS accumulation in the CM and then removed the murepavadin by washing before converting the whole cells to spheroplasts and exposing these to colistin alone. The murepavadin pre-treated spheroplasts were much more susceptible to colistin-induced CM damage and lysis than untreated spheroplasts (Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7.

claim: A sub-lethal concentration of murepavadin sensitised P. aeruginosa PA14 to a normally sub-lethal concentration of colistin (2 µg ml−1), resulting in >10,000-fold reduction in c.f.u. counts relative to bacteria incubated with murepavadin or colistin alone after 8 hr.
source: We found that a sub-lethal concentration of murepavadin sensitised P. aeruginosa PA14 to a normally sub-lethal concentration of colistin (2 µg ml−1), resulting in >10,000-fold reduction in c.f.u. counts relative to bacteria incubated with murepavadin or colistin alone after 8 hr (Figure 5A).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In 11 out of 14 murepavadin-susceptible CF isolates tested (79%), sub-lethal concentrations of murepavadin caused a significant increase in the bactericidal activity of colistin against P. aeruginosa.
source: In 11 out of 14 murepavadin-susceptible CF isolates tested (79%), sub-lethal concentrations of murepavadin caused a significant increase in the bactericidal activity of colistin against P. aeruginosa (Figure 5B).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Murepavadin did not affect the bactericidal activity of colistin against the strain that was resistant to the LptD inhibitor.
source: Importantly, murepavadin did not affect the bactericidal activity of colistin against the strain that was resistant to the LptD inhibitor (Figure 5B).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Mono-therapy with colistin alone or murepavadin alone had very little effect on the bacterial load assessed after 3 hr treatment compared with the no-treatment control in a murine lung infection model.
source: Mono-therapy with colistin alone or murepavadin alone had very little effect on the bacterial load assessed after 3 hr treatment compared with the no-treatment control (Figure 5C).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Combination therapy with colistin and murepavadin caused a ~500-fold reduction in c.f.u. counts relative to the no-treatment control in a murine lung infection model.
source: By contrast, combination therapy with colistin and murepavadin caused a ~500-fold reduction in c.f.u. counts relative to the no-treatment control (Figure 5C).
evidence: This experimental result is directly stated and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Colistin-mediated disruption of the cytoplasmic membrane is considerably less efficient than that of the outer membrane.
source: In support of this, whilst colistin induced OM damage within minutes of bacterial exposure to the antibiotic, disruption of the CM took much longer. Even when spheroplasts lacking an OM were exposed to colistin, it still took more than 2 hr for CM permeabilisation to occur. Therefore, it appears that colistin-mediated disruption of the CM is considerably less efficient than that of the OM, likely due to the much lower levels of LPS present in the CM.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experimental observations comparing the kinetics of OM versus CM disruption.

claim: The abundance of LPS in the cytoplasmic membrane of P. aeruginosa was found to be ~100 times lower than the outer membrane.
source: Similar to Salmonella and E. coli, the abundance of LPS in the CM of P. aeruginosa was found to be ~100 times lower than the OM, indicating that only about 1% of total LPS is present in the CM (Zendo et al., 2010; Osborn et al., 1972).
evidence: This observation is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The presence of low concentrations of LPS (1% total composition) in phospholipid bilayer membranes was both necessary and sufficient for colistin-mediated permeabilisation.
source: However, studies with model membranes have shown that the presence of low concentrations of LPS (1% total composition) in phospholipid bilayer membranes was both necessary and sufficient for colistin-mediated permeabilisation (Khadka et al., 2018).
evidence: This finding is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Murepavadin is a first-in-class peptide-based inhibitor of the LptD component of the LptABCDEFG complex of P. aeruginosa.
source: Murepavadin is a first-in-class peptide-based inhibitor of the LptD component of the LptABCDEFG complex of P. aeruginosa that transports LPS from the CM to the OM (Andolina et al., 2018).
evidence: This description is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Inhibition of the Lpt system in P. aeruginosa leads to LPS accumulation in the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: Thus, inhibition of the Lpt system in P. aeruginosa leads to LPS accumulation in the CM, which we hypothesised would increase the susceptibility of the bacterium to colistin (Andolina et al., 2018; Sperandeo et al., 2008).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Colistin damages the cytoplasmic membrane by disrupting cation bridges between LPS molecules.
source: In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that colistin targets LPS in the CM of polymyxin-susceptible E. coli, leading to the displacement of cationic inter-LPS bridges, membrane disruption, and ultimately bacterial lysis.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experimental data showing magnesium protection and is consistent with the known mechanism at the outer membrane.

claim: The high levels of LPS modified by pEtN in the cytoplasmic membrane of MCR-1-producing E. coli prevent colistin from targeting LPS in the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: However, the high levels of LPS modified by pEtN in the CM of MCR-1-producing E. coli prevent colistin from targeting LPS in the CM, protecting the membrane and conferring resistance to the polymyxin antibiotic.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experimental data showing the relationship between LPS modification and colistin resistance.

claim: MCR-1 protects the cytoplasmic membrane but not the outer membrane from colistin-mediated permeabilisation.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that MCR-1 protects the CM but not the OM from colistin-mediated permeabilisation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experimental data showing differential protection of the two membranes.

claim: LPS is the cytoplasmic membrane target of colistin.
source: Therefore, since MCR-1 specifically modifies LPS and this modification selectively protects the CM from colistin in a dose-dependent manner, we concluded that LPS is the CM target of colistin, just as it is in the OM.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experimental data showing the specificity of MCR-1 protection and dose-dependent relationship.
